lesson.title: Strong Correlation, Weak Argument: Correlation Versus Causation
lesson.summary: A high correlation coefficient measures only the strength of a linear association and never by itself proves that one variable causes the other, since lurking variables can produce equally strong correlations.
lesson.body:
It is tempting to treat a large correlation coefficient as proof of a cause-and-effect relationship, especially when the number is striking. But r measures one thing only: the strength and direction of a linear association between two variables. It contains no information about which variable, if either, is causing the other to change, and no information about whether some third factor is responsible for both. This gap between what r measures and what people often want it to mean is exactly where correlation-causation confusion is born.

The firefighter example from lurking variables makes this concrete. The correlation between number of firefighters dispatched and property damage across five hypothetical fires came out to r = 0.988, about as strong a linear association as real data ever produces. If correlation implied causation, this would mean dispatching fewer firefighters causes less damage, so a fire department could reduce property losses by sending fewer trucks. That conclusion is absurd, and everyone recognizes it as absurd, precisely because both variables are actually driven by a lurking variable, the size of the fire, and neither firefighters nor damage is causing the other.

The general principle behind this example is worth stating plainly: correlation, no matter how close to 1 or -1, is consistent with several different underlying explanations. The two variables might be linked by direct causation (x causes y), by reverse causation (y actually causes x), by a lurking variable driving both, or by simple coincidence in a limited data set. A correlation coefficient cannot distinguish among these explanations; it only confirms that a linear pattern exists in the data. Notice that r = 0.988 in the firefighter example is numerically almost identical to what a genuinely causal relationship might produce, which is exactly the trap: the size of r gives no hint at all about which of the four explanations is the correct one.

The way to move from correlation toward a causal claim is not to compute a bigger or more precise correlation, since even a perfect correlation of 1.0 would not settle the question. Instead, causation requires the kind of evidence discussed under causation itself: a randomized experiment in which the researcher, not nature, decides who gets which treatment, breaking any link between the treatment and pre-existing lurking variables. Short of that, the honest and correct statement about an observed correlation, no matter how strong, is that the two variables are associated, with a described strength and direction, and that other explanations for that association, including lurking variables, cannot be ruled out from the correlation alone.

Keeping "correlation" and "causation" as separate claims, backed by separate kinds of evidence, is one of the most consequential habits in all of statistics, because so many misleading headlines and policy arguments rest on quietly sliding from one to the other without ever earning the upgrade. Learning to notice that slide, in a news article, an advertisement, or your own reasoning about a strong r value, is one of the most transferable skills this entire unit on regression diagnostics has to offer.
